El radón es un elemento químico perteneciente al grupo de los gases nobles. En su forma gaseosa es incoloro, inodoro e insípido y en forma sólida su color es rojizo. En la tabla periódica tiene el número 86 y símbolo Rn. Su masa media es de 222, lo que implica que por término medio tiene 222-86 = 136 neutrones. Igualmente, en estado neutro le corresponde tener el mismo número de electrones que de protones, esto es, 86. Es un elemento radiactivo y gaseoso, encuadrado dentro de los llamados gases nobles. El radón es producto de la desintegración del radio (226Ra), elemento altamente radiactivo. El isótopo 219Rn es producto de la desintegración del actinio, llamado actinón y tiene una semivida de 4 segundos. Además de todos estos, el radón tiene 22 isótopos artificiales, producidos por reacciones nucleares por transmutación artificial en ciclotrones y aceleradores lineales. El isótopo más estable es el 222Rn, también el más abundante, con una semivida de 3,8 días y producto de la desintegración del 226Ra. Al emitir partículas alfa se convierte en 218Po. Aplicaciones: La emanación del radón del suelo varía con el tipo de suelo y con el contenido de uranio superficial, así que las concentraciones al aire libre del radón se pueden utilizar para seguir masas de aire en un grado limitado. Este hecho ha sido puesto al uso por algunos científicos atmosféricos. Aunque algunos médicos creyeron una vez que el radón se puede utilizar terapéuticamente, no hay evidencia para esta creencia y el radón no está actualmente en uso médico, por lo menos en el mundo desarrollado. El sismólogo italiano Gianpaolo Giuliani había anticipado el terremoto que sacudió la zona central de Italia el 6 de abril de 2009 y basó sus pronósticos en las concentraciones de gas radón en zonas sísmicamente activas, fue denunciado a la policía por "extender la alarma" y se vio obligado a quitar sus conclusiones de Internet. Un mes antes del terremoto de una magnitud de entre 5,8 y 6,3 en la escala de Richter que habría dejado unas 50.000 personas sin techo, alrededor de 26 ciudades sufrieron daños graves y más de un centenar de muertos, unas furgonetas con altavoces comenzaron a circular por L'Aquila (Italia) pidiendo a sus habitantes que evacuaran sus casas, después de que el sismólogo anticipara que se produciría un gran terremoto. https:// es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radón

IMSS resguarda 25 mil expedientes históricos en archivo de 38 años El archivo histórico del IMSS cumple 38 años con 25 mil expedientes, fotografías, planos y documentos que preservan la historia de la seguridad social en México. Por Gabriela Díaz | Reportera El Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (IMSS) conserva 25 mil expedientes históricos, alrededor de 60 mil fotografías y cuatro mil planos que documentan la evolución de la salud y la seguridad social en México. El acervo se encuentra en el Centro Único de Información y Archivo Histórico “Ignacio García Téllez”, que este 16 de noviembre cumple 38 años de preservar documentos fundamentales para reconstruir la historia de la institución y del sistema de seguridad social mexicano. Ubicado en el Centro Médico Nacional Siglo XXI, el recinto también cuenta con más de 30 mil documentos digitalizados, una biblioteca especializada, hemeroteca, videos y carteles disponibles para consulta pública. Un archivo nacido tras los sismos El proyecto comenzó en 1985, por instrucciones del entonces director general del IMSS, Ricardo García Sainz , ante la necesidad de identificar y concentrar documentos históricos que permanecían dispersos en diferentes edificios y áreas administrativas. Los sismos de septiembre de ese año aceleraron los trabajos, debido a que parte de los archivos se encontraba en inmuebles afectados por los movimientos telúricos. Para rescatar y concentrar los materiales se habilitó un espacio que anteriormente funcionaba como estacionamiento en el Centro Médico Nacional Siglo XXI. En 1988 se formalizó la creación del Centro, que integró la Biblioteca Central Médica, el Centro de Documentación y el Archivo Histórico Institucional. Documentos únicos de la historia del IMSS Entre las piezas de mayor valor histórico se encuentra el contrato que firmó el muralista Diego Rivera , además de registros de la primera contabilidad gubernamental del Instituto y fotografías relacionadas con la construcción de sus hospitales. El archivo también conserva imágenes de la presentación del proyecto arquitectónico del Hospital La Raza a Ignacio García Téllez , figura fundamental en los antecedentes de la seguridad social mexicana y cuyo nombre identifica este recinto. El titular de la División de Administración de Documentos del IMSS, Marco Antonio Orozco Zuarth , explicó que mantener este patrimonio requiere labores permanentes de clasificación, descripción, organización y conservación, realizadas por personal especializado. “La preservación de todos estos documentos es un trabajo constante, minucioso, persistente, que casi no se nota, pero que se hace día a día”, señaló. Digitalización e inteligencia artificial El proceso de conservación también incluye la digitalización de documentos para facilitar su consulta y reducir la manipulación de los originales, con lo que se busca prolongar su vida útil. Actualmente, el Instituto cuenta con más de 30 mil documentos digitalizados. Sin embargo, uno de los siguientes objetivos consiste en incorporar tecnología más avanzada e inteligencia artificial para agilizar las búsquedas y ampliar las posibilidades de consulta en línea. Orozco Zuarth indicó que estos trabajos se han desarrollado con recursos institucionales y requieren continuidad para ampliar el acceso al patrimonio documental. –sn– Sociedad Noticias ¡Conéctate con Sociedad Noticias ! BREAKING: Everything A few hours ago, I went to rent a Lime bike to ride the ten minutes to my therapy appointment. I opened Lime, scanned the QR code, and double clicked my iPhone’s side button to authorize Apple Pay. The app hung for a few moments, then closed. I tried several more times and the same thing happened. In the back of my mind, I wondered what was going on — was the Lime bike broken? Was my cell phone service out? Was it something else? I opened the Uber app and, similarly, wasn’t able to pay. I opened DownDetector and realized that the entirety of Apple Pay , a thing I thought existed only on my phone and not the cloud, was down. I texted my therapist, put my phone in my pocket, and started jogging. Not being able to rent a Lime Bike for several minutes is an extremely minor inconvenience barely worth mentioning. And yet the mental gymnastics my brain did in those few minutes — what’s broken, why is it broken, how is it broken — is something that everyone I know have been repeatedly doing for the last few weeks as seemingly every service and system crashes down around us. Over the weekend, people who I do not normally talk to about my job asked me: What is going on with the airplanes ? Why is my bank down ? What about Microsoft ? The default assumption that many people are making is that these are either being caused by cyberattacks and/or “AI” broadly defined, whether that’s AI gone haywire, “rogue” AI agents, or something else, which is indicative of just how fearful people are of AI . What I have been telling people is, basically, that shit is broken and things are going to keep breaking. For lots of different reasons. It’s often not a hack and it’s often not explicitly AI-related, but everything now sort of looks like that XKCD comic of the dependency domino tower . While not exactly true that AI and cyberattacks are causing these outages, it’s also not entirely wrong, either. What we’re seeing is — I think — a series of infrastructure failures (and some cyberattacks) that are not directly connected but are broadly a symptom of the same general trends and systemic problems we’ve seen across society, the government, and the tech sector over the last several years. First, it’s worth mentioning that anytime there’s a string of outages, there’s a tendency to tie them altogether. And outages or hacks that previously wouldn’t have been noted at all suddenly get more attention and become part of the narrative. Take, for example, the fact that the International Ice Hockey Federation has been targeted by a cyberattack; you probably would not normally hear about this but it has suddenly become part of the broader story . The simplest explanation I can come up with for the broader disastrous trend we’ve seen is that since the pandemic we have seen: mass layoffs of tech workers and software developers mass deployment of AI-assisted and vibe coded products, software updates, and patches mass layoffs in the government sector and outright destruction of government expertise and oversight the loss of institutional knowledge associated with those layoffs and funding cuts a failure to invest in upgrading infrastructure/redundancy government contracts handed out to the President’s friends and political allies AI and LLM-assisted/iterative exploit discovery, coding, and deployment companies responding to the AI hacking threat with AI-coded and rushed patches When Elon Musk took over Twitter and named it X, there were many people who thought his layoffs and the associated loss of expertise would result in the site failing basically because of an infrastructural failure. Twitter would basically “go down” because someone would break something and no one would know how to fix it. We haven’t really seen that happen to X, but that same philosophy of firing the experts and YOLOing AI into everything while hoping shit doesn’t break is now the explicit strategy of our entire economy and our entire government. What we are seeing, then, is a mix of tightly clustered attacks, outages, and fuckups that you would expect to see when people and companies are careless, don’t know what they’re doing, or are working very fast to respond or duct-tape something together in the face of new threats. "We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure" We know that this is happening to some extent because, in the aftermath of the PHP2Shell exploit, which was discovered with the assistance of LLMs, we saw various websites go down as they attempted to push updates faster than they normally would have to, because the time between a vulnerability being discovered and it being exploited is faster than ever. (As I was writing this, Calif, one of the companies that used LLMs to find PHP2Shell, announced that it had used LLMs to find apparently serious vulnerabilities in Java .) Companies and agencies are pushing updates (including to, for example, our air traffic control system) on live systems, in part because of the threat of AI, and things are breaking. The National Security Agency, for example, said earlier Tuesday that some internal systems went down because of “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” Nick Andersen, the acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency , said Tuesday that we need to build more resilience into our infrastructure, but building resilience and redundancies into software requires people who understand how systems can possibly fail, planning for it, and mitigating against it. “Ultimately being able to prevail by being able to demonstrate resilience against disruptions, whether they occur because of things like an IT outage or a bad patch, or a modernization update gone awry, or because of a malicious malicious cyber incident — we want to make sure we’re engineering in the resilience that is going to be able to anticipate for and ultimately overcome those outages and those impacts,” Andersen said at an event called FedTalks. We may eventually get to a place where expertise and understanding highly complex systems is once again a priority, but the last few years have been full of companies and governments moving incredibly fast to reduce reliance on humans and offload it to AI systems and AI-generated code in order to ostensibly save money on labor costs and/or carry out an antihumanist political project. I thought this piece, called “ Software is breaking down at a systemic level ,” written by a software developer named Jimmy Breck-McKye, was quite good. He points at Kristen Maevyn’s The Decoherence Trap , which argues that AI-written code is causing a situation where people and companies do not understand their products. “Most software engineers now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent — they just can’t keep on top of the complexity,” Breck-McKye writes. “Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels — we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole.” People increasingly don’t understand or have any idea how their code works, people are moving very fast, and bad things are happening. Any individual outage or breakdown is likely, to some extent, a coincidence. Many of the outages we are seeing have nothing to do with AI at all, but do have something to do with the broader lack of investment in infrastructure, redundancy, and expertise. We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure and so, I guess, we must simply continue to expect bad things to happen.

# extinction "The Extinction of the Javan Rhino: Beyond Natural Disasters... Concerns over the survival of the Javan rhino have often been linked to threats from natural disasters, such as eruptions from Mount Anak Krakatau and the subsequent tsunamis. However, the risk of extinction for this endemic species from Indonesia is not solely due to natural factors. Human activities and other factors also loom large. So, what are these factors? (. . .) Ali elaborated that to tackle these issues, conservation efforts must focus on the root causes of population decline. This approach not only aims to save threatened individual wildlife. 'This can be achieved by protecting and restoring habitats, strengthening patrols and enforcing laws, maintaining connectivity between habitat areas, and monitoring population health,' Ali stated. In order for all efforts to succeed, he emphasized the need for multi-stakeholder involvement, ranging from the government, private sector, to local communities. In principle, preventing extinction is not just about protecting the animals; it is also about ensuring that habitats and environmental conditions that support their survival are maintained. ' In this way, the wildlife population (including Javan rhinos) can survive and reproduce naturally for extended periods,' Ali asserted. Furthermore, according to Yulinda, various issues must be addressed through audits and transparency. She acknowledges that extinction may occur due to poor governance, such as budget limitations, inconsistent population data, and indications of individuals' involvement in poaching cases. 'The solution involves audits, data transparency, and consistent judicial rulings. In the case of horn trade, for instance, an intermediary was acquitted at the first level, and the prosecutor filed for cassation. Inconsistent rulings weaken the deterrent effect,' she emphasized." https:// go.kompas.com/read/2026/11/17/ 213005974/the-extinction-of-the-javan-rhino-beyond-natural-disasters
